title: Whistleblower

jokes.text: There is nothing wrong, nor will there ever be wrong, with any Sabre printers. Case closed.
jokes.setup: The episode opens mid-crisis — Sabre printers are catching fire and making news.
jokes.punchline: Michael's absurdly overconfident declaration that closes a case that is very much open, delivered with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: A strong cold-open beat. 'Case closed' is perfectly Michael — he uses authoritative language he has no authority to back up. Character integration is the joke's strength.

jokes.text: I saw you on the news and I want to pinch your tiny wiener.
jokes.setup: Packer calls Michael after seeing him on the news, which feels like a moment of professional recognition.
jokes.punchline: The compliment is immediately revealed to be a crude, Packer-brand sexual taunt about Michael's genitalia.
jokes.explanation: Pure Packer — the joke only works because it's him. The subversion from 'recognition call' to lewd insult is quick and effective. The word 'tiny' does a lot of work. Somewhat cheap but perfectly character-specific.

jokes.text: Oh! Pac-Man, I thought you were a girl.
jokes.setup: Michael answers a call from Packer while Jo and the office are watching.
jokes.punchline: Michael's delighted response reveals he initially thought a woman was calling him, which is inexplicably baffling and very Michael.
jokes.explanation: A small but perfectly Michael non sequitur. The confusion is unexplained and therefore funnier. Doesn't land huge but adds texture.

jokes.text: And then I call Froggy 98.7, their request line. I talked to the host about it on the air.
jokes.setup: Michael is describing his media blitz in response to being on local news.
jokes.punchline: He escalates his self-promotion to calling a radio station's *request line* — the line for song requests — to talk about the printer scandal.
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of the 'request line' is what makes this. Michael doesn't call the station; he calls the request line. That specificity reveals his cluelessness beautifully and economically.

jokes.text: I am officially the second most watched clip of the day on the WBRE news site. / What's number one? / Oh? That teacher who was wrongfully accused of being a pedophile. / Now, we cannot let the pedophile win again.
jokes.setup: Michael brags about his viral moment on local news.
jokes.punchline: 'We cannot let the pedophile win again' — the phrase 'win again' implies this is a recurring rivalry, and Michael frames a wrongly accused pedophile as his competitor.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The structure is near-perfect: the straight question ('What's number one?') opens the door, the answer is already absurd (wrongly accused pedophile), and then Michael adds the devastating kicker: 'again' — implying this isn't the first time he's lost to this man. 'The pedophile win again' is a quotable, highly specific comic construction. Earns its dark edge.

jokes.text: So, instead of working, you want... Yes. Okay. Yes.
jokes.setup: Michael asks everyone to watch his clip 11 times instead of working.
jokes.punchline: Jim starts to articulate the absurdity of the request, Michael confirms with no shame, and Jim accepts it with defeated compliance.
jokes.explanation: A well-worn Office rhythm (Jim protests, Michael doubles down) but executed cleanly. The 'Yes. Okay. Yes.' has good comic timing. Not transcendent but reliably effective.

jokes.text: Oh! Did you see this report that the zoo got a baby otter? / Aw! It's kissing its mommy.
jokes.setup: Michael just asked everyone to watch his serious media appearance 11 times.
jokes.punchline: Instead, they find a baby otter video on the same site and immediately abandon Michael's request for something cuter.
jokes.explanation: Solid situational comedy. The pivot from Michael's ego to a baby otter is a clean undercut. Nothing exceptional but it serves the scene well.

jokes.text: Really? A baby otter? Okay, count me in as 'Who cares?'
jokes.setup: The office is cooing over a baby otter video.
jokes.punchline: Michael dismisses it with forced indifference, only to immediately be proven a hypocrite by the next beat.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'count me in as Who cares' is a funny, specific Michael-ism. His subsequent melting over the otter makes it retroactively funnier.

jokes.text: It can't even stand up. It's trying to stand up. / There he goes.
jokes.setup: Michael declared he didn't care about the baby otter.
jokes.punchline: Michael is now narrating the otter's attempts to stand, fully invested. The scene holds for over 30 seconds of implied silent otter-watching.
jokes.explanation: The callback to his 'who cares' dismissal lands well. The visual of the whole office silently watching a baby otter for a full 30 seconds is the real joke — a long, earned comedic beat. 'There he goes' has lovely quiet triumph. Rewatch value because the silence plays differently knowing the setup.

jokes.text: There he goes. [Long silence until 02:17]
jokes.setup: Michael and employees have been watching the baby otter attempt to stand
jokes.punchline: The entire office goes silent for nearly 30 seconds watching the otter — a visual gag inferred from the long gap before the next dialogue
jokes.explanation: The 28-second gap between 'There he goes' and the next scene is the joke — the entire office, during a crisis, silently watching an otter learn to walk. The economy is perfect: three words and then silence does more than a monologue. Strong rewatch value because you know to look at everyone's faces.

jokes.text: Jo arrives unannounced at the Scranton branch.
jokes.setup: The entire office has been watching a baby otter video instead of addressing the PR crisis.
jokes.punchline: Jo walks in mid-otter-watch; the implied scramble and mortification is entirely visual and inferred.
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe setup — authority figure arrives to catch employees goofing off. Functional but not distinctive.

jokes.text: Put your hand up, Norma Rae. / If you say anything, so help me God, I'll break off the temples of your glasses and stick them in your eye sockets.
jokes.setup: Jo asks if anyone talked to the press. Dwight catches Angela about to raise her hand.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's threat is wildly disproportionate and anatomically specific — 'the temples of your glasses' shows he's thought this through.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'temples of your glasses' is what elevates this above a generic threat. Dwight has pre-planned the exact mechanics of the assault. Pure Dwight. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Even if I thought that our printers killed baby seals, I would not be a whistleblower. The Bernards, for generations, have silenced whistleblowers. It's how we made all our money.
jokes.setup: Characters are establishing their loyalty or disloyalty.
jokes.punchline: Angela reveals her family's entire fortune is built on silencing whistleblowers — a perfectly dark, surprising family backstory.
jokes.explanation: Angela's rigid, authoritarian family history is excellent character comedy. The phrase 'It's how we made all our money' is delivered as mundane fact, which is the joke. Her commitment to the bit and the dark specificity make it work.

jokes.text: Woody Guthrie wrote a song about us. Old Mister Bernard / Who have you silenced today?
jokes.setup: Angela has just said her family silenced whistleblowers for generations.
jokes.punchline: She escalates by citing a Woody Guthrie protest song written specifically about her family — and hums/sings a line from it.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional escalation. The Woody Guthrie reference is perfectly chosen — he's the archetypal protest folk singer — making the Bernards the ultimate corporate villains. Hearing Angela hum 'Old Mister Bernard / Who have you silenced today?' as a cheerful folk tune is a brilliantly absurd image. Rivals the 'pedophile' joke as the episode's standout. High quotability and strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: There is no reason for anyone here to sign this because I know everything there is to know about these people. I know when their birthdays are, I know what their favorite kind of cake is, I know what color streamers they like. / All that's just birthday information, Michael.
jokes.setup: Michael claims deep personal knowledge of his employees as proof of their innocence.
jokes.punchline: His 'deep knowledge' turns out to be exclusively birthday party logistics, which Jo correctly labels 'birthday information.'
jokes.explanation: A tight, well-structured joke. Michael's self-delusion about the depth of his employee relationships is perfectly captured — his 'knowing everything' is tricolons of party data. Jo's deadpan correction ('that's just birthday information') is a perfect straight-man line.

jokes.text: When Mama was working as a prison guard, and something went missing, she'd ask one question: 'What do we do when we find the guilty party?' And if they said, 'Come down on them with that swift hammer of justice,' innocent. A clear conscience don't need no mercy.
jokes.setup: Jo is explaining her interrogation philosophy to Michael.
jokes.punchline: The logic is essentially backwards folk wisdom — professing belief in harsh punishment proves innocence — delivered with complete maternal certainty.
jokes.explanation: Good Jo characterization. Her prison-guard Mama backstory is vivid and the inverted logic is funny, but it's a bit wordy and the payoff doesn't fully land relative to the setup length.

jokes.text: But if they said, 'Officer Bessie, well, they may have had a reason.' Blah, blah, blah, blah... Well, nine times out of 10, that's the anus they checked.
jokes.setup: Jo is completing her prison-guard interrogation theory.
jokes.punchline: 'That's the anus they checked' — a graphic prison procedure delivered with the casual warmth of a grandmother sharing a recipe.
jokes.explanation: The punchline earns its shock value because of how matter-of-factly Jo delivers it. The contrast between her genteel Southern manner and the clinical prison-guard detail is the joke. 'That's the anus they checked' is memorably specific.

jokes.text: We should give them a one-way ticket to Montego Bay. Where they keep all the al-Qaeda. / Uh, that's Guantanamo Bay.
jokes.setup: Michael is asked what punishment should befall the whistleblower.
jokes.punchline: Michael's malapropism — confusing Montego Bay (a Jamaican resort) with Guantanamo Bay — while confidently asserting that's 'where they keep all the al-Qaeda.'
jokes.explanation: Michael's geographic/political confusion is a classic well-executed character beat. The specific wrong answer (a beach resort) makes it funnier than a generic gaffe would be. Jo's flat correction lands well.

jokes.text: I want these people to really pay. I want them to suffer. / I'd prefer it if they died.
jokes.setup: Michael and Jo are discussing what to do with the whistleblower.
jokes.punchline: Michael's escalation from 'suffer' to preferring death — said with absolute sincerity and then immediately justified as a moral stance.
jokes.explanation: Solid escalation beat. Michael's willingness to go straight to capital punishment is funny but not the sharpest version of this joke type.

jokes.text: Dwight, what the hell? Apache persuasion hold, that's the hell.
jokes.setup: The IT guy asks Dwight to let him into a computer; Dwight has apparently grabbed him
jokes.punchline: Dwight has put the IT guy in a wrestling hold — the 'Apache persuasion hold' — as a casual workplace interaction
jokes.explanation: The naming of the hold — 'Apache persuasion hold' — is perfectly Dwight. The casual application of a wrestling maneuver to a routine workplace request is good physical comedy. The IT guy asking 'what the hell' and Dwight answering 'Apache persuasion hold, that's the hell' is a great comedic rhythm.

jokes.text: Dwight applies the 'Apache persuasion hold' on the IT guy to get access to his computer.
jokes.setup: The IT guy is at his computer when Dwight needs access.
jokes.punchline: Dwight has a named, self-invented physical hold for this exact scenario — 'Apache persuasion hold' — implying a whole taxonomy of Dwight maneuvers.
jokes.explanation: The named hold is quintessential Dwight. He doesn't just move someone aside — he has a formal technique with a name. The 'Apache' prefix adds cultural absurdity. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: No, that's cool. Sometimes I run. / I'm a runner.
jokes.setup: Dwight has clearly found something incriminating on Kevin's computer.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's cover story — that he 'runs' — is so implausible coming from Kevin that it's the punchline. He then redundantly reinforces: 'I'm a runner.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. The humor entirely depends on knowing Kevin. His desperate, unconvincing excuse — followed by the insecure restatement — is pitch-perfect. 'I'm a runner' as a standalone declaration from Kevin is beautifully absurd. High character integration.

jokes.text: Everybody, we are at DEFCON 5. / Everybody knows it was Andy, and it is not fair for us all to take the fall for his big, stupid mouth.
jokes.setup: Angela is furious about the leak investigation affecting everyone.
jokes.punchline: Angela — who was nearly the leak herself (Dwight stopped her from raising her hand) — righteously blames Andy with complete hypocrisy.
jokes.explanation: The irony is richer on rewatch. Angela's performative outrage about Andy is funny given her own near-confession. The hypocrisy is the joke but it requires context to land fully.

jokes.text: And like I'm going to believe one of his spurned lovers.
jokes.setup: Angela is accusing Andy of being the leak.
jokes.punchline: Dwight dismisses Angela's testimony by calling her Andy's 'spurned lover' — which is both accurate (they briefly dated) and delivered with complete contempt, ignoring that Dwight himself is Angela's ex.
jokes.explanation: Dwight using 'spurned lover' as a disqualifier, from a place of complete emotional blindness to his own situation with Angela, is layered and character-specific. Works on multiple levels for fans of their arc.

jokes.text: Good boy. You turning that money into more money? / Are you referring to alchemy?
jokes.setup: Jo compliments Michael on having a good year financially and asks if he's investing.
jokes.punchline: Michael interprets 'turning money into more money' as literally referring to alchemy — the medieval pseudoscience of turning base metals into gold.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully concise. Michael's confusion is somehow both too stupid and too erudite — he knows the word 'alchemy' but applies it wrong. The deadpan delivery makes it work perfectly. One of the more quotable Michael lines in the episode.

jokes.text: I'm not dumb, I'm smart. / Well, buy property. That's my advice.
jokes.setup: Jo has called Michael 'dumber than a dummy' for not investing in property.
jokes.punchline: Michael's indignant 'I'm not dumb, I'm smart' is the least convincing self-defense possible, followed by Jo's deflating non-sequitur 'buy property.'
jokes.explanation: Functional. 'I'm not dumb, I'm smart' is on-brand for Michael but not a particularly original construction. Jo's pivot is good but the whole exchange is minor.

jokes.text: I swear on the graves of my parents who aren't even dead yet.
jokes.setup: Jo doesn't believe Andy's denial that he leaked the story.
jokes.punchline: Andy swears on his parents' graves — but immediately clarifies they're not dead yet, undermining the oath while somehow intending it to strengthen it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The construction is clever: the oath is meant to signal sincerity, but Andy immediately undermines it with a factual correction that makes it meaningless — and yet he seems to think the clarification *strengthens* the oath. This is absurdist logic that's entirely character-consistent. Highly quotable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in terms of economy and misdirection.

jokes.text: Did you tell anyone outside of this office that the printers were catching on fire? / Yeah, I did. / I was talking to this girl at a bar. I think she could sense my sadness. And I found out too late that she was a copyeditor at the Trib.
jokes.setup: Jo interrogates Darryl directly, clearly expecting denial.
jokes.punchline: Darryl immediately confesses, then reveals his leak was pillow talk with a woman he was trying to impress — who turned out to be a newspaper editor.
jokes.explanation: The immediate confession is funny (subverts interrogation genre expectations), and 'she could sense my sadness' is a quietly poignant comic detail. 'I found out too late' implies tragic timing. Solid storytelling.

jokes.text: Was she cute? / No. Oh, God, Darryl.
jokes.setup: Darryl has just confessed to leaking company secrets to a journalist.
jokes.punchline: Michael's only follow-up question is whether the journalist was attractive. Jo's exasperated response speaks for everyone.
jokes.explanation: Three words from Michael ('Was she cute?') perfectly capture his priorities in a crisis. Jo's flat 'No. Oh, God, Darryl' packages two reactions in four words. Maximum economy. A very efficient comedic exchange.

jokes.text: And now he's probably going to get fired for it. And if that is not poetic justice, I don't know what is.
jokes.setup: Michael is upset that Darryl, one of his best employees, is now at risk of being fired for the leak.
jokes.punchline: Michael calls Darryl being fired 'poetic justice' — a phrase that means the opposite of what Michael intends, since justice would involve the *guilty* being punished, which is exactly what's happening. But Michael thinks Darryl is innocent.
jokes.explanation: Michael misusing 'poetic justice' when it actually applies correctly is a nice double-layer but probably flies over casual viewers' heads. Modest laugh.

jokes.text: Except this. / Wow. This is just a mystery novel that I've been working on. / I know what it is. I skimmed the first chapter.
jokes.setup: Jo says they found nothing on Michael's computer — and then produces something.
jokes.punchline: It's a mystery novel Michael is writing, and Jo has already read enough of it to have an opinion.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the following joke; functional but not particularly funny on its own.

jokes.text: I'm just curious, why would a man who hates people want to have a relationship with a maid? / I don't know... / The way I look at it, there's only one of two reasons. He knows a secret about her that she doesn't know herself. Or he wants to use her services to mop up after a murder.
jokes.setup: Jo has read Michael's mystery novel and is critiquing the protagonist's motivations.
jokes.punchline: Jo offers two possible explanations for the hero's interest in the maid — the second being that he intends to use her to clean up a murder scene.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'mop up after a murder' — using the maid's literal function as a weapon — is a good absurdist turn. Jo's sincere delivery of literary analysis that concludes with murder makes it work. 'Write your own damn novel' as Michael's response is also a solid button.

jokes.text: Write your own damn novel.
jokes.setup: Jo has just offered unsolicited plot analysis of Michael's mystery novel.
jokes.punchline: Michael's indignant dismissal frames a genuine author's frustration — he doesn't want Jo to solve his own book for him.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words, completely on character. Michael treating his unfinished mystery novel as a sacred creative work is funny. The button is crisp.

jokes.text: I'm talking to this woman at day care, she's telling me all about her amazing trip to Vietnam. I have nothing. I tell her our printers catch on fire spontaneously.
jokes.setup: Pam confesses she was the second leak.
jokes.punchline: Her motivation: social competition with a daycare mom. She had nothing to contribute so she revealed a corporate scandal to seem interesting.
jokes.explanation: Wonderfully relatable and character-specific. The social anxiety of having nothing to say at a daycare conversation and compensating with a corporate scandal is both true to Pam's character and sharply observed social comedy. 'I have nothing' is the honest, funny heart of it.

jokes.text: This is a very good idea. This is good. Let's get all the bad ideas out now. Flush them out.
jokes.setup: Pam is panicking and suggesting she tell Jo or Michael about her leak.
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'sarcastic encouragement' framing — calling her panic 'ideas' that need to be 'flushed out' — is dry Jim at his best.
jokes.explanation: Reliable Jim-deadpan beat. The 'flush them out' framing is a nice touch. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: My mind is going a mile an hour. / That fast?
jokes.setup: Pam is panicking about what to do about the leak.
jokes.punchline: Jim's deadpan 'That fast?' gently mocks Pam's inadvertently low bar for mental speed.
jokes.explanation: Two words. One of the most economical jokes in the episode. 'A mile an hour' is already an accidentally self-deprecating idiom, and Jim's 'That fast?' turns it into a perfect micro-zinger. Works on paper, works even better with Krasinski's delivery. High quotability, excellent economy.

jokes.text: I always thought Darryl and Pam might get me fired for something I said.
jokes.setup: Michael has just discovered he has two whistleblowers instead of one.
jokes.punchline: His talking-head confessional reveals his fear has always been that THEY would get HIM fired — inverting the moral culpability completely.
jokes.explanation: Good confessional beat. Michael's assumption that the danger to him would come from his own offensive statements (rather than legitimate corporate wrongdoing) is very true to character.

jokes.text: I weirdly know exactly what you're saying to me. So, I'll see you in Meredith's van in five minutes. / Okay, you didn't need to actually say that.
jokes.setup: Michael is communicating covertly with Jim about meeting the leakers.
jokes.punchline: Michael's idea of a covert signal is to literally say exactly what the covert meeting plan is out loud, and Jim points out the obvious failure.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael incompetence joke — he understands the *concept* of subtlety without understanding how to execute it. Jim's correction is the clean punchline.

jokes.text: I have never seen so many parking tickets. / All right, this is just messed up. / No, you know what's messed up? This situation all up in here is what's messed up.
jokes.setup: The conspirators are meeting in Meredith's van.
jokes.punchline: The van is apparently a disaster zone of parking tickets — an implied running visual gag about Meredith's chaotic life spilling over into this scene.
jokes.explanation: A decent background visual gag about Meredith's lifestyle. Not fully developed; the parking tickets are mentioned and dropped.

jokes.text: Hey, guys, sorry I'm late. / We're not going for yogurt.
jokes.setup: Ryan arrives late to the secret van meeting.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's cheerful obliviousness ('sorry I'm late') is met with Michael's baffling 'we're not going for yogurt' — implying Ryan somehow thought this was a yogurt run.
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny — the yogurt non sequitur suggests a whole separate social dynamic (Michael and Ryan regularly get yogurt?). Doesn't fully land but has a good weird energy.

jokes.text: Guys, I couldn't help it. It is so boring where we work. I mean, it's as interesting as a morgue. / It might be less interesting than a morgue. / Hey, hey, it's as interesting as a morgue.
jokes.setup: Ryan is confessing to being a leak too, explaining he can't stop talking.
jokes.punchline: Michael cannot allow Ryan to call their workplace LESS interesting than a morgue — he insists on the equivalency.
jokes.explanation: Michael's indignant defense of a morgue comparison is a perfect absurd priority inversion. He's hurt that Ryan implied even a morgue has more going on. The 'Hey, hey' correction is great.

jokes.text: I can't control what I say to people. I spend the whole day talking. I mean, I video chat, I skype, I text, I tweet, I phone, I woof. / Woof is a site that I'm launching to be the last word in social networking.
jokes.setup: Ryan explains why he leaked — he can't stop communicating.
jokes.punchline: Ryan has invented his own social network called 'Woof' and is pitching it mid-crisis, in a van, to people who need his help.
jokes.explanation: Completely Ryan. His grandiose tech startup delusion in the middle of a crisis is perfect character comedy. 'Woof' as a social network name is deliberately bad in a funny way.

jokes.text: For just $12.99 a month, Woof links up all your communication portals, so you are always within reach. It's part of the dog pack, as I call it. But look, why tell you, when I can show you? I just sent myself a woof. / Ryan, you have a woof on line one. / Thank you, Erin. / Woof!
jokes.setup: Ryan is pitching his Woof social network in the middle of a crisis meeting.
jokes.punchline: He has apparently pre-arranged a demo with Erin, who announces 'You have a woof on line one' with total professionalism, and Ryan receives it by barking 'Woof!'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional escalation payoff. Ryan has pre-briefed Erin to play along with the Woof demo, Erin delivers 'you have a woof on line one' with complete straight-faced professionalism, and Ryan responds 'Woof!' It's beautifully layered: Ryan's self-delusion, Erin's earnest participation, and the bark as a functional notification sound. One of the episode's best jokes. High quotability, rewatch value.

jokes.text: Okay, here's what we do. I say we just smash all the computers. We destroy the evidence. No evidence, no case. / Wouldn't we get fired for smashing all the computers? / No, okay, not all the computers. Just our computers.
jokes.setup: The group needs a plan to avoid being caught.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's plan is to smash all computers; when challenged, he immediately pivots to 'just our computers' as if that's the reasonable amendment.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's criminal naivety is funny and consistent. The escalation from 'all computers' to 'just our computers' as a concession is good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Mike, you know you don't have to turn us all in. All you need is one scapegoat. / Uh, if you turn me in, I'm turning in Darryl. / That's just what we need, another black man in prison, you know?
jokes.setup: The group is negotiating who might be sacrificed as the scapegoat.
jokes.punchline: Darryl deflects with racial politics — framing turning him in as a social justice issue — which is simultaneously self-aware and transparently self-serving.
jokes.explanation: Darryl using systemic racial injustice as a very personal shield is both pointed and funny. The joke works because Darryl is entirely self-aware that he's being self-serving — the humor is in the brazenness.

jokes.text: If you turn me in, I'm turning in Darryl. That's just what we need, another black man in prison, you know?
jokes.setup: Ryan threatens to expose Darryl if exposed himself
jokes.punchline: Ryan immediately undercuts his own threat by acknowledging the racial injustice implication — 'another black man in prison' — with complete Ryan-level obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Ryan's self-awareness of the optics without actually changing his threat is very Ryan Howard. The meta-commentary on racial disparity delivered while making a threat is simultaneously woke and deeply cynical — good dark comedy.

jokes.text: Let me give you a hand. Ready? On three. / Oh, shoot.
jokes.setup: Michael and Jo are apparently dealing with some physical task (implied from context: getting up from chairs, or a handshake ritual).
jokes.punchline: The 'Oh, shoot' implies something went wrong in a comedic physical moment.
jokes.explanation: Without visual context this is very hard to assess. As written/subtitle-only it's minimal. Likely a physical bit that plays better on screen but doesn't translate to transcript.

jokes.text: The property you're looking at is in great shape. By the way, it has a very spacious basement office. / Basement office? You mean like a lair?
jokes.setup: Dwight is pitching a property to Jo, trying to sell a building feature.
jokes.punchline: Jo reframes 'basement office' as a 'lair,' implying she knows exactly what Dwight would use it for.
jokes.explanation: Jo's immediate 'lair' reframe is a sharp character observation about Dwight. It's quick, precise, and reveals Jo has Dwight's number. Good economy.

jokes.text: I was up all lunch thinking about what we should do to this individual. You know what I think we should do? We make them come to work. And we work them, and we make them sit next to all the people they screwed over. And we pay them, but we make them feel like they did something really wrong.
jokes.setup: Michael is proposing his punishment plan for the whistleblower to Jo.
jokes.punchline: Michael's maximum punishment is... a normal job, with a Christmas bonus. This is what Michael thinks constitutes workplace torture.
jokes.explanation: Superb character joke. Michael's 'punishment' for the whistleblower is literally just continued employment — normal work, a salary, a Christmas bonus. The gap between his framing ('make them feel really wrong') and the mundane 'punishment' is the entire joke. It accidentally reveals that Michael's idea of hell is a normal office job, which resonates darkly with the whole show's premise. High character integration — this ONLY works as Michael. Strong rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: The one question I have is, 'Do we give them a Christmas bonus?' I say yes, it's Christmas, but right after, they're back into the thick of it.
jokes.setup: Michael has outlined his 'punishment' of normal employment
jokes.punchline: He deliberates about the Christmas bonus — ultimately decides yes, but stresses they're right back to normal employment immediately after
jokes.explanation: The bonus deliberation adds another layer to Michael's 'punishment' joke — he can't help being a good boss even when trying to be punitive. 'It's Christmas' as a non-negotiable ethical position is very Michael.

jokes.text: Michael Scott. / What? / It doesn't matter what I know. / If it doesn't matter, then tell me.
jokes.setup: Jo finally confronts Michael directly, addressing him by full name.
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately defeats the logic of 'it doesn't matter what I know' by pointing out that if it doesn't matter, she should just tell him.
jokes.explanation: Michael accidentally makes a logically valid point. Mildly funny, more of a transitional beat than a standout joke.

jokes.text: Are you gonna kill me?
jokes.setup: Jo has told Michael to 'come with me' without explanation and led him somewhere alone
jokes.punchline: Michael's genuine fear that Jo might murder him — delivered as a sincere question
jokes.explanation: Good beat — Michael's anxiety and dramatic imagination lead him to the murder hypothesis. The sincerity of the question is the joke. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Are you gonna kill me?
jokes.setup: Jo has wordlessly driven Michael somewhere unknown, neither explaining nor speaking.
jokes.punchline: After a long tense silence, Michael's first concern is whether he is about to be murdered.
jokes.explanation: Four words. Perfect economy. Michael's willingness to immediately go to 'murder' scenario is consistent with his dramatic personality. The beat of silence before it lands sells it. Punches above its weight due to timing.

jokes.text: I just need you to come by later and sign a few forms. / Okay. What time works for you? / Mr. Schrute? What time works?
jokes.setup: Jo has mysteriously driven Michael somewhere — he thought he might be murdered.
jokes.punchline: She just needs him to sign forms. Dwight materializes out of nowhere to also ask about timing.
jokes.explanation: The deflation from 'murder' to 'sign forms' is good, and Dwight's sudden appearance asking about scheduling is a nice throwaway. The bit about Dwight potentially buying Jo's building is the real subtext.

jokes.text: Cancel it. I want you to make an offer at 1725 Slough Avenue. Make them an offer they can't refuse. No, on second thought, lowball them.
jokes.setup: Jo has just made a Godfather reference ('make them an offer they can't refuse').
jokes.punchline: She immediately undercuts the cinematic menace by switching to 'lowball them' — revealing she's just a shrewd businesswoman, not a mob boss.
jokes.explanation: The Godfather setup and the 'lowball them' pivot is a clean misdirection. Works well as a Jo character beat — she speaks in grand terms but is ultimately pragmatic.

jokes.text: With the chief of police.
jokes.setup: Michael has been nervously explaining he has an early dinner he can't miss during this mysterious drive.
jokes.punchline: He drops 'with the chief of police' as a name-drop that reveals he's either actually important or wildly deluded — and either way is funny in the moment.
jokes.explanation: Brief, economy-driven joke. The name-drop is very Michael. Short and punchy.

jokes.text: I'm very relieved to learn it wasn't you.
jokes.setup: Jo has been conducting interviews to find the leak.
jokes.punchline: Stan (a background character) denies it, and Jo takes his denial at face value with a hilariously sincere 'I'm very relieved.'
jokes.explanation: Small throwaway joke about Jo's odd sincerity toward background staff. Mild chuckle.

jokes.text: What a rich timbre your voice has.
jokes.setup: Stan, a background character, has said 'It wasn't me' in a possibly distinctive voice.
jokes.punchline: Jo's non sequitur compliment on his voice is an absurd aside that reveals her eccentric sensibility.
jokes.explanation: Jo's random vocal appreciation is an odd, funny character beat. 'Rich timbre' is an unexpectedly elevated phrase in this context.

jokes.text: Okay, I am prepared to conclude the investigation. / And? / You did it. / What? Based on what? / Just all the evidence. And it really seems like it was you.
jokes.setup: Dwight has been investigating the leak, and Andy is under suspicion.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's conclusion — 'just all the evidence' and 'it really seems like it was you' — is maximum vagueness dressed as authoritative certainty.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's prosecutorial pomposity meeting zero substance is a classic Dwight bit. 'Just all the evidence' is perfect bureaucratic non-answer. Good.

jokes.text: Can we all agree to say that it was Andy for now and sit with it, see how it feels?
jokes.setup: Dwight has concluded Andy did it without real evidence.
jokes.punchline: His proposal to 'sit with it and see how it feels' applies the language of emotional processing to a false accusation, which is absurdly inappropriate.
jokes.explanation: The therapeutic framing of a scapegoating — 'sit with it, see how it feels' — is a great incongruous language choice. Dwight applying mindfulness to false accusation is a strong specific joke.

jokes.text: Yeah, you know? I mean, for all we know, it could have been Jim. / Really?
jokes.setup: People are protesting framing Andy; Oscar defends him.
jokes.punchline: Oscar then immediately pivots to randomly suggesting Jim, who gives a 'really?' camera look — a classic mockumentary beat.
jokes.explanation: Jim's camera look is a well-worn Office tool but always effective. Oscar's sudden pivot from defending Andy to throwing Jim under the bus is a good character beat — Oscar's self-interest emerging.

jokes.text: I bought a video camera last year and I was looking at the tapes, and there were only, like, 12 minutes that I felt was worth taping. The whole year. And most of that was just birds in my condo complex.
jokes.setup: Jo is continuing to share the small disappointments of her year.
jokes.punchline: A whole year of life produces only 12 minutes of footage worth keeping, and most of that is birds.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's genuinely great jokes. The detail is so specific and the implication so bleak — a powerful, successful woman has 12 minutes of meaning in a year, mostly birds — that it transcends mere comedy to become a quietly devastating observation about loneliness and success. 'Most of that was just birds in my condo complex' is the kind of detail that great comedy writers find. It recontextualizes Jo's whole character in seconds.

jokes.text: And I miss Holly.
jokes.setup: Jo is sharing her personal disappointments in a vulnerable moment.
jokes.punchline: Michael abruptly redirects the emotional conversation to his own longing — 'And I miss Holly' — perfectly inserting his feelings into someone else's confession.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum character. Michael's inability to maintain focus on anyone else — even during a CEO's emotional admission — is perfectly rendered. The 'And I miss Holly' is so organically Michael's non sequitur that it becomes charming rather than annoying. Also plants the seed for the episode's emotional payoff. Economy score 9.5 — among the most efficient jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: And I miss Holly. Who's Holly? Holly Flax. From the Nashua branch. Best HR rep that Dunder Mifflin has ever seen.
jokes.setup: Michael opens up about missing someone in the context of Jo's vulnerability
jokes.punchline: The buildup and Michael's sincere description of Holly as 'best HR rep Dunder Mifflin has ever seen' — his romantic feelings expressed entirely in professional terms
jokes.explanation: Michael expressing love through professional accolades is very on-brand. The episode's emotional core is also here — the Holly thread will pay off. The sincere delivery makes it both funny and touching.

jokes.text: It has not been a blockbuster year for me financially. My Blockbuster stock is down.
jokes.setup: Characters are sharing their disappointments.
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'blockbuster year' idiom is immediately literalized — he actually owns Blockbuster stock.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect wordplay joke. Michael uses the idiom 'blockbuster year,' then immediately reveals he means it literally because he holds Blockbuster stock — which in 2010 was cratering toward bankruptcy. The literalization of the metaphor is perfect, and the Blockbuster stock specificity dates it in a way that's now even funnier in retrospect. Economy is exceptional — one sentence does everything. Rivals the episode's top jokes.

jokes.text: I may have heard from an old client and I may have immediately started spreading the news to other clients and potential clients, yeah. But I'm not here to talk about that. I'm here to talk about Suck It.
jokes.setup: Michael is pressed about whether he spread information about the printer fires.
jokes.punchline: Michael half-confesses to being a leak himself, then pivots to promoting 'Suck It' — his own failed business venture — treating corporate espionage as a PR opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Michael casually admitting to being a leak while pivoting to his startup is perfectly oblivious. The 'Suck It' pivot — using Gabe's leak investigation moment as a product pitch window — is classic Michael ego.

jokes.text: Gabe, I told you all about the printers. / I mean, it could be you, Gabe. / Yes, it's totally obvious. I mean, that's the point. / I think we all can agree it's either Gabe or Angela. / It's Angela. Get her, boys.
jokes.setup: Gabe is conducting a meeting to uncover the leak.
jokes.punchline: Michael steamrolls Gabe's investigation by first accusing Gabe, then immediately pivoting to Angela, then directing an attack with 'Get her, boys.'
jokes.explanation: 'Get her, boys' is a great Michael escalation — he's appointing himself mob boss of the accusation. The rapid pivot from Gabe to Angela with zero evidence is very Michael.

jokes.text: It's Angela. Get her, boys.
jokes.setup: Michael is naming suspects
jokes.punchline: 'Get her, boys' — Michael apparently has boys to deploy, directed at Angela
jokes.explanation: The pure confidence of 'Get her, boys' — particularly without knowing who the boys are — is a funny Michael moment. Brevity helps.

jokes.text: Hey, guys. Sorry to interrupt. I just wanted to say goodbye to everyone. Through Teach For America, I'm going to go down to Detroit and teach inner-city kids about computers.
jokes.setup: In the middle of the tense leak investigation, the IT guy Nick appears to say a heartfelt goodbye.
jokes.punchline: The earnestness of his 'Through Teach For America' moment is about to be destroyed by the room's complete indifference.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the more potent jokes that follow. Nick's hopeful exit is the straight man being loaded.

jokes.text: Phyllis, what's this guy's name again? / I don't know. Is it Shadow or Garth? It's something weird, I... / My name is Nick.
jokes.setup: Nick is saying a heartfelt goodbye after months of working at the office.
jokes.punchline: Michael doesn't know Nick's name — and neither does Phyllis, who guesses 'Shadow or Garth.'
jokes.explanation: Phyllis guessing 'Shadow or Garth' is the most specific and funniest part — it implies she's been calling him wrong things for months. Nick's 'My name is Nick' lands with quiet devastation.

jokes.text: Okay, well, 'Nick,' we're in a meeting. / Okay, look, I get it, people. I'm the lame IT guy and everybody hates me.
jokes.setup: Nick has just identified himself by name to people who don't know it.
jokes.punchline: Michael puts 'Nick' in air quotes — doubting the name he was just told — and Nick breaks down with naked self-awareness: 'I'm the lame IT guy and everybody hates me.'
jokes.explanation: Michael putting 'Nick' in air quotes is an inspired escalation — he refuses to accept the name at face value. Nick's self-aware breakdown is cringe comedy well executed.

jokes.text: Hey, listen, man, you can't take it personally. / You call me 'man'? I just said my name, just now. Did you forget it already? / No, sport.
jokes.setup: Darryl tries to console Nick.
jokes.punchline: Nick calls out that Darryl immediately forgot his name to use 'man' — and Michael's response to this accusation is 'No, sport,' proving Nick's point.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating callback. Nick specifically calls out the name-amnesia, and Michael immediately confirms it by using yet another generic substitute ('sport'). The structure is airtight: accusation → proof of accusation in real time. 'No, sport' is a great punchline. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor in economy and escalation.

jokes.text: You guys have 15 parties a week. You can't learn my name? / Hey, hey, hey, IT guy. Here's the story, champ. None of us have spent a lot of time getting to know you, okay? We liked the last guy, Sadiq, because he kept to himself. And we also thought he might have been a terrorist.
jokes.setup: Nick is confronting the office about not knowing his name.
jokes.punchline: Michael's defense of not knowing Nick is that the *previous* IT guy was better because he was invisible — and they liked him because they suspected he was a terrorist.
jokes.explanation: Michael delivers one of his finest speeches. 'We liked the last guy, Sadiq, because he kept to himself. And we also thought he might have been a terrorist' is a perfect Michael line: casually offensive, weirdly logical (suspicion made him interesting), and completely self-unaware. The 'IT guy' / 'champ' usage continues the name-refusal theme. One of the episode's best. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Here's the story, champ. None of us have spent a lot of time getting to know you, okay? We liked the last guy, Sadiq, because he kept to himself. And we also thought he might have been a terrorist.
jokes.setup: Michael tries to explain the office's relationship with IT staff
jokes.punchline: They liked Sadiq because he kept to himself — and also they suspected him of terrorism, which apparently endeared him
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. The office preferred the previous IT guy because (1) he kept to himself and (2) they suspected him of terrorism — two completely different scales of 'reason to like someone' treated as equivalent. Michael saying this while trying to CONSOLE Nick makes it perfect. 'We also thought he might have been a terrorist' as a compliment is inspired dark comedy.

jokes.text: You know what? I'm going to leave you with one other thought. Inner-city kids use computers for two things, games and porn. So, good luck wasting your life, Lurch.
jokes.setup: Nick is making his exit speech, having ostensibly tried to take the moral high ground.
jokes.punchline: He abandons the high road to savage the office, undersell inner-city education, and call Michael 'Lurch' — finally getting the last word and using a nickname himself.
jokes.explanation: The callback is the gem: Nick has been a victim of everyone else's nicknames, so his exit move is to deploy a nickname of his own ('Lurch'). The cynical dismissal of his own Teach for America mission ('inner-city kids use computers for games and porn') subverts his earlier idealism. 'Good luck wasting your life' is a great zinger. Strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: Thank you so much for that.
jokes.setup: Nick has just demolished Michael with 'good luck wasting your life, Lurch.'
jokes.punchline: Michael's genuinely gracious 'Thank you so much for that' — either he didn't process the insult or he took it as a compliment.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to the Nick sequence. Michael's warmly sincere response to being insulted is pure character — he's either too dim to register it or too needy to turn down any kind of attention. Maximum economy, maximum character.

jokes.text: I saw all of your hard drives. And guess what? You're not a photographer. And you definitely can't fit into a size two.
jokes.setup: Nick is delivering parting shots to the office based on what he found on their computers.
jokes.punchline: Unnamed office employees are exposed for vanity delusions — someone thinks they're a photographer, someone thinks they wear a size two.
jokes.explanation: Funny escalating burn sequence. The specific accusations (photographer, size two) feel targeted at recognizable character types and land as broad but effective comedy.

jokes.text: Darryl, man, you're on Facebook. Why have you been telling people you're not on Facebook? People want to be your friend, man.
jokes.setup: Nick is burning people with hard-drive knowledge.
jokes.punchline: Darryl has been secretly on Facebook while denying it — a weirdly relatable and specific social media lie.
jokes.explanation: The Facebook denial is both era-specific and a recognizable personality type — someone who wants to seem too cool for social media while secretly using it. 'People want to be your friend, man' is a nicely sympathetic accusation.

jokes.text: And you... This guy. You're the one who told the press. You wrote an e-mail to the editor. I saw it and I also saw a Quicktime movie of your little printer fire test on your hard drive. This guy's the snitch, he's the snitch.
jokes.setup: Nick is on a roll exposing everyone's hard drive secrets.
jokes.punchline: Nick unexpectedly solves the entire episode's mystery — identifying Andy as the actual leak — turning his exit speech into the investigation's resolution.
jokes.explanation: Structurally satisfying — the episode's 'throwaway' departing IT guy becomes the deus ex machina that solves the plot. 'This guy's the snitch, he's the snitch' as the accusation from the least-respected person in the office is a good ironic reversal.

jokes.text: When I was growing up, there was nothing better than being a big old business tycoon. And I thought I'd break that glass ceiling and be a hero to all those little girls out there. And they'd make a Barbie out of me.
jokes.setup: Jo is sharing her backstory and aspirations
jokes.punchline: Jo's ultimate dream — a Barbie made in her image — is simultaneously understandable for a woman of her generation and bathos
jokes.explanation: Jo's Barbie dream is both genuinely moving and funny — a powerful CEO's ultimate metric of success is a toy doll. The character depth here is good, and the Barbie detail is specific enough to be truly funny.

jokes.text: When I was growing up, there was nothing better than being a big old business tycoon. And I thought I'd break that glass ceiling and be a hero to all those little girls out there. And they'd make a Barbie out of me.
jokes.setup: Jo is revealing her vulnerabilities about her public image in a confessional.
jokes.punchline: Jo's lifelong dream distills to a Barbie being made in her image — a specific, childlike goal that's both touching and absurd.
jokes.explanation: Jo's Barbie aspiration is characterful and specific. The contrast between corporate titan and childhood toy ambition is funny and oddly humanizing. Good character work.

jokes.text: Nobody will want to play with my Barbie.
jokes.setup: Jo has explained that a public recall apology would permanently define her legacy.
jokes.punchline: The corporate consequence is expressed as 'nobody will want to play with my Barbie' — a CEO's worst fear articulated in the language of a child.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and character joke. Jo's boardroom-level crisis is reduced to a child's playground concern. The sentence is perfectly constructed — the incongruity between the speaker, the stakes, and the language is maximally funny. One of the episode's standout moments. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Well, you know, I would be willing, under the right circumstances, to do that for you. / Oh, honey, surely you don't want that. / I surely do, and don't call me honey.
jokes.setup: Jo has said she would hate to be the one to make a public apology.
jokes.punchline: Michael volunteers to take the press hit — and when Jo says 'honey, surely you don't want that,' Michael fires back with 'I surely do, and don't call me honey' — a clear Airplane! reference.
jokes.explanation: The Airplane! reference lands for those who catch it, and even without it the inversion of Michael demanding not to be called 'honey' is funny given his general need to be liked. Good economy.

jokes.text: Airplane II.
jokes.setup: Michael has just made an Airplane! reference ('I surely do, and don't call me honey').
jokes.punchline: He announces the reference himself — 'Airplane II' — immediately deflating his own cool moment by over-explaining it and getting the film wrong.
jokes.explanation: Two words that do extraordinary work. Michael ruins his own callback by (a) announcing it, (b) attributing it to the wrong film. It's a joke about Michael's inability to be cool, executed in the fewest possible syllables. Economy score 10 — one of the most efficient jokes in the episode. High character integration: only Michael would do this.

jokes.text: I own a one-eighth share in a rental property down in Pittston. / Well, I'm one-eighths proud of you.
jokes.setup: Dwight reports his property investment following Jo's advice
jokes.punchline: Jo's 'one-eighths proud' — proportionally calibrating her pride to match his fractional investment
jokes.explanation: 'One-eighths proud of you' is a near-perfect joke — economy is essentially maxed. Jo matching the fraction exactly as a proportional response is the kind of specific wordplay that becomes highly quotable. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: I own a one-eighth share in a rental property down in Pittston. / Well, I'm one-eighths proud of you.
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to relate to Jo as a fellow property investor, having just been advised to buy property.
jokes.punchline: Jo's 'one-eighths proud of you' perfectly mirrors his fractional ownership — it's a calibrated compliment that is also a massive diss.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest jokes in the episode. Jo's proportional pride is a perfect structural callback to Dwight's fractional share — the math does the comedy. 'One-eighths proud of you' is immediately quotable and the construction is elegant. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in structure and economy.

jokes.text: Enjoy that chair for now. 'Cause pretty soon you will be on your feet. / Like Buckingham Palace.
jokes.setup: Dwight is hinting at his plan to buy Jo's building and become her landlord.
jokes.punchline: Jo's response 'Like Buckingham Palace' — after Dwight's threat about being 'on her feet' — is a non sequitur that implies she finds Dwight's posturing royally absurd.
jokes.explanation: The Buckingham Palace reference is a bit opaque and doesn't land as cleanly as surrounding jokes. Minor beat.

jokes.text: Hey, Phyllis, have you seen my bag? / You deserve it.
jokes.setup: Andy casually asks Phyllis about his missing bag.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis, believing Andy is the whistleblower who caused all the trouble, responds to his mundane question with a moral verdict: 'You deserve it.'
jokes.explanation: Three words in response to a question about a bag, carrying the full weight of office moral judgment. The economy is exceptional — Phyllis doesn't explain, doesn't rant, just delivers her verdict and moves on. The mismatch of the mundane question with the grand moral response is perfectly constructed. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Look, I didn't want houses and schools to burn down and children to die. / Does that make me a hero? / No, it does not. / Well, it doesn't make me the worst guy in the world, either. / It does!
jokes.setup: Andy is doing a talking-head confessional about his motivations for going to the press.
jokes.punchline: Andy's attempt to claim hero status is immediately denied, then he lowers the bar to 'not the worst guy in the world' — also denied, more emphatically.
jokes.explanation: Classic escalating denial structure. Andy lowering the bar from 'hero' to 'not the worst' only to have that also refused is well-constructed. Darryl's 'It does!' is a perfect button — immediate and emphatic.

jokes.text: Andy? Hey. I wanted to say that I think it was very brave of you to go to the press.
jokes.setup: Andy has just been revealed (correctly) as a leaker and Michael knows it.
jokes.punchline: Michael compliments Andy on 'bravery' for going to the press — but Michael himself has been ranting about wanting the leaker to suffer and die. The sincerity is dissonant.
jokes.explanation: Decent reversal — Michael's 180 from 'I want them to die' to 'very brave' is consistent with his need to be liked and his impulsive emotional swings. But it's understated and doesn't get a big laugh.

jokes.text: Andy? Hey. I wanted to say that I think it was very brave of you to go to the press. / Thanks. Yeah, you know. Just seemed like the right thing to do.
jokes.setup: Pam knows Andy didn't actually do it but was given credit; she compliments him
jokes.punchline: Andy accepts credit for heroism he didn't actually commit — 'just seemed like the right thing to do' — completely comfortable with false glory
jokes.explanation: Good irony — Pam is guilty and complimenting Andy for heroism he didn't perform; Andy accepts without question. The silent awkward beat after (long gap to 20:38) amplifies it.

jokes.text: 'We at Sabre have betrayed the trust that we have built with our customers... There will be no questions.' Are there any questions?
jokes.setup: Michael is reading a prepared press statement that explicitly ends with 'There will be no questions.'
jokes.punchline: Michael finishes the statement and immediately invites questions — either not reading the last line or ignoring it entirely.
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-structured joke. The setup is embedded in the statement text itself, so the punchline is self-contained. Michael undermining his own press statement by inviting questions is both character-true and logically satisfying.

jokes.text: That was fun.
jokes.setup: Michael has just read a crisis recall statement to the press on behalf of Sabre.
jokes.punchline: His immediate reaction is 'That was fun' — treating a PR crisis as a performance opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly encapsulate Michael's relationship to public spectacle. His genuine delight at being on camera — regardless of the context — is the show in miniature. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: Okay. Hey, you could transfer Holly back from Nashua. / Let me see what I can do.
jokes.setup: Jo has offered to 'brighten Michael's life' as thanks for taking the press hit.
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately cashes in the goodwill chip not for a raise or promotion, but to get Holly transferred back — revealing his real priority.
jokes.explanation: Strong emotional callback to the Holly admission mid-episode. Michael's use of a major corporate favor to pursue a personal romantic goal is consistent and sweet. 'Let me see what I can do' from Jo — casually granting what Michael has wanted all season — is a satisfying payoff. Rewatch value because of its arc implications.

tmdb_overview: Michael is surprisingly cheerful after learning some bad news about Donna. The new parents, Pam and Jim, have trouble staying awake in the office. Meanwhile, Angela takes matters into her own hands when Dwight refuses to honor their contract.
